title: Q&A with Radhika Gupta & Mohnish Pabrai - May 29, 2020
summary: An Edelweiss Connect conversation during the COVID lockdown. Pabrai explains why he moved from running an IT company to investing (aligning his outer life with his hardcoded 'inner map'), the low-risk Dhandho nature of entrepreneurship, focusing on the downside first, and the Microsoft-in-1999 lesson that a great business at 75x earnings is a poor investment. He argues lockdowns caused permanent economic damage that markets are not pricing in, criticizes India's self-inflicted economic wounds, and discusses leverage as his biggest mistake, the Buffett lunch, bridge, success, asset management in India and philanthropy.

ideas.idea: Each person's inner map is hardcoded by age five and never changes; the sliver of humans who align their outer life with it go very far.
ideas.detail: Two industrial psychologists gave him his 'owner's manual' in 1999 at age 34, three months before Pabrai Funds launched, and said they could not understand how he functioned running a 160-person IT company; one became an original investor. He now keeps his calendar with no scheduled calls or meetings.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take big risks; ignoring venture-backed startups (under 0.1% of all startups), they seek low-risk arbitrage with limited downside.
ideas.detail: A dry cleaner opening a small, short-lease drop-off shop in a new town between two existing towns can scale if it works and pull back if it does not; Dhandho, his Gujarati roommate's word, means an approach to business with upside and no downside.

ideas.idea: The first question about any investment is 'How would I lose money on this?'; focus on the downside and the upside takes care of itself.
ideas.detail: The checklist comes later to ensure nothing is missed; the aim is investments where the downside is very muted.

ideas.idea: Microsoft in 1999 at a $600 billion cap and 75x trailing earnings was obviously a bad investment despite being a great business, and stayed flat for 14-15 years with a 50%-plus drawdown.
ideas.detail: He told Microsoft employees with 90% of net worth in the stock to trim; paying $600 billion for $6-7 billion of earnings takes too long to earn back at any growth rate. Twenty years later at $1.2 trillion the return was about 3.5% a year ex-dividends, 5% with.

ideas.idea: The FANGs are unbelievable businesses with moats and pricing power, but it is all baked into ridiculous trailing P/Es, so the odds are against investors buying them today.
ideas.detail: Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Google and Netflix are driving the S&P; you could buy Amazon and look great in 10 years, but it is not a good bet.

ideas.idea: Leverage is the number one reason value investors' investments fail; he now avoids levered businesses and financial institutions and uses no margin.
ideas.detail: In 2008-09 with 10 positions making up 80% of assets, a mortgage lender went to zero and another finance company nearly did, taking a while to recover from. The other big failure causes are management/ownership ethos and misunderstanding the moat.

ideas.idea: History will judge leaders poorly for COVID shutdowns because nobody analyzed the cost of 35 million lost US jobs against 100,000 deaths.
ideas.detail: Suicide, depression, divorce, domestic violence and child abuse will rise; India's mass migrations made social distancing impossible; masks and distancing are good, but wholesale shutdowns were the wrong call.

ideas.idea: Businesses are fragile creations, and the shutdown destroyed hundreds of thousands that will never return, causing permanent damage to the global economy.
ideas.detail: The US normally loses 1,600 businesses a week (100,000 a year) and creates more; from 3% unemployment and 160 million employed in January 2020, it may take five to ten years to get back, not this year, not next, not when everyone is vaccinated.

ideas.idea: US markets have brushed off COVID and are not pricing in the bad news; the polarization between FANGs/Tesla and languishing brick-and-mortar resembles 1999-2000.
ideas.detail: Markets assume a vaccine in finite time (historically vaccines have never come this fast) and no further shutdowns; he guesses 7-8% US unemployment two years out. The US is a superhuman economy that will bounce back, and some brick-and-mortar businesses are decent values.

ideas.idea: India inflicts self-wounds: it captured almost none of the manufacturing exodus from China that Vietnam picked up because its rules defy Ricardo and Adam Smith.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: The mantra for making a country rich is well known from Lee Kuan Yew, Pinochet's Chicago School economists, Adam Smith and Ricardo; vote-bank politics prevents it, and India could be lifting tens of millions from poverty every year but is not.

ideas.idea: Once you have a roof and three meals, it is dumb to get hyperactive about wiggles in the stock market; if wealth is lost, nothing is lost.
ideas.detail: The drivers of happiness and good health are not brokerage balances; keep perspective except for those truly without food.

ideas.idea: He bid for the Buffett lunch purely as guru dakshana to thank Buffett for intellectual property that made him tens of millions, and it paid dividends through friendships with Buffett and Munger.
ideas.detail: Buffett set no time limit and the lunch ran over three hours with his daughters aged 10 and 12 and Guy Spier; it led to many bridge games and dinners with Munger. Buffett wants winners to feel they got a bargain.

ideas.idea: Bridge and investing are both games of probabilities, which is why so many value investors play; COVID showed there are no sure things, only fat tails.
ideas.detail: He plays five to six hours a week on Bridge Base, Buffett more than 10; he once played online with Buffett.

ideas.idea: Success means leading an aligned life daily, being happy, and being liked, admired and trusted, not just the financial output.
ideas.detail: He cites Buffett's test of whether friends would hide you like the Jewish girl in World War II; bridge, blackjack, investing and even Dakshana are math games he wants to play elegantly.

ideas.idea: In India, look for businesses with long runways and aligned management that can do well assuming the government does nothing.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: India grows at night while the government sleeps; the mantra is the same anywhere, great moat plus great management with the right incentives. Jio's execution in taking share and resetting pricing has been amazing, though he is not recommending the stock.

ideas.idea: Indian asset and wealth management has incredible multi-decade tailwinds as money moves out of gold, real estate and fixed deposits into equities.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: US frictional costs have fallen through technology and scale while India's remain high; buy a home to live in, not for price appreciation. He is a shareholder of Edelweiss and its wealth and asset management franchises excite him most.

ideas.idea: Investors do themselves a disservice through hyperactivity; you make money by waiting.
ideas.detail: High frictional costs plus hyperactivity hurt investor results both in the US and India.

ideas.idea: Capitalism maximizes wealth but not balanced wealth, so government and philanthropy must redistribute without damaging the engine, which India gets backwards.
ideas.detail: India clobbers its wealth-creation engine and then redistributes a pie that is not growing; Americans are the most generous people on earth and private foundations like Gates do far better work than governments.

ideas.idea: Book recommendations: Greenspan's 'Capitalism in America' (from Munger, with lessons for India) and Richard Koo's 'The Other Half of Macroeconomics' (from Li Lu) on why money printing did not cause inflation.
ideas.detail: Munger recommended the Greenspan book at their last dinner on March 7, 2020, a week before US lockdowns.
